implementation_notes: `java.lang.ThreadLocal<T>` (since 1.2) is the carrier: each thread gets an independently initialized copy, `withInitial`/`initialValue` supplies lazily created per-thread objects, and `remove()` is mandatory when pooled threads reuse the value. The JDK itself uses the technique - `ThreadLocalRandom.current()` (since Java 7) keeps PRNG state per thread - and stack confinement needs no API at all: locals that never escape are safe. Use it for genuinely thread-scoped state; on virtual threads and structured scopes the per-thread map becomes a memory problem and `InheritableThreadLocal` does not inherit into structured forks, so new context-passing code should prefer ScopedValue (the sibling variant) while ThreadLocal stays correct for per-thread caches and mutable state.
pitfalls: Forgetting remove() on a pooled thread leaks the value and its classloader - the classic application-server redeploy leak - and the next task sees stale data.
InheritableThreadLocal only copies when a thread is created with new Thread(...); thread pools and StructuredTaskScope forks do not inherit, so the child silently sees null.
A ThreadLocal holding a heavyweight object (request-scoped buffers, connections) multiplies memory with virtual threads; it is not a pooling mechanism.

variants.name: ScopedValue (Java 25, structured sharing)
variants.implementation_notes: A ScopedValue (final in Java 25, JEP 506) is write-once per dynamic scope: the value is bound for the execution of a lambda and reverts automatically, so there is no remove() and no unbounded lifetime - the javadoc's API note contrasts exactly these three ThreadLocal problems (mutation, unbounded lifetime, expensive inheritance). Child threads forked from a StructuredTaskScope created inside the scope inherit the binding without copying, which is what makes per-request context scale to virtual threads; the bound value must be immutable or safely published. It cannot host mutable per-thread caches and does not replace ThreadLocal where state is genuinely thread-scoped.
pitfalls: Bindings are inherited only by threads started in a structured scope created inside the binding (javadoc: inheritance is limited to such structured cases); legacy executors do not see the value.
There is no set(): a callee cannot modify the caller's value, so two-way context propagation still needs ThreadLocal or explicit state.
Scoped values are meant to be few - the per-thread lookup cache defaults to 16 entries - so many cyclically used keys degrade get() performance.
